name: Carignan

lines.s10: Carignan is the old vine red of the Languedoc: black raspberry and cranberry, dried thyme, and a bite of acidity and tannin together.
lines.s20: Carignan is a Mediterranean red that keeps high acidity and firm tannin even in great heat. Old vines in the Languedoc, Spain and Sardinia give it depth: black raspberry, cranberry and dried thyme, in a wine made for rich, rustic food.
lines.s45: Carignan was long the workhorse of the Languedoc, and old hillside vines have made its name. It tastes of black raspberry, cranberry and dried cherry, with dried thyme and liquorice. It is deep in colour, with high acidity and firm, rustic tannin. Many cellars ferment the berries whole in a sealed vat, which softens that grip. The Languedoc and Spain tend to be savoury, while old vines in Chile and California are often juicier and more openly fruity. Pour it with cassoulet, grilled sausages or lamb. Spain, where it most likely began, calls it Cariñena or Mazuelo, and old vine growers in Chile share one name for theirs, Vigno.
lines.sale: Carignan is the red with bite: black raspberry, dried thyme and a freshness that keeps a rich, slow cooked dish lively. With the cassoulet, the duck or the sausages, it is the bottle I would bring.

glass.lead: Black raspberry, cranberry and dried cherry with dried thyme, liquorice and a note of iron, deep in colour, high in acidity and tannin.

ladder.where: Maule in Chile and the high hills of Corbières
Roussillon, Priorat, Sulcis in Sardinia and Contra Costa

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, tannin high and rustic, alcohol medium plus, body medium to full.

old.where: Languedoc and Roussillon; Priorat, Montsant and Rioja; Sulcis in Sardinia
old.glass: Tends to be savoury and firm: black raspberry, cranberry and dried cherry with dried thyme, liquorice and iron, high acidity and rustic tannin. Old vine Priorat and Sulcis are typically darker, riper and denser.
old.cellar: Mostly a partner in blends with Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre; in the Languedoc often fermented whole, by carbonic maceration, to soften the tannin. Rioja uses a little, as Mazuelo.

new.where: Maule in Chile; Mendocino, Sonoma and Contra Costa in California
new.glass: Typically juicier and purer in fruit: damson, dark cherry and cranberry with a little dried thyme, the same high acidity and a firm but finer grip.
new.cellar: Usually bottled under the grape's name, from old, dry farmed bush vines: in Maule some as VIGNO, in California often from old mixed vineyards with Zinfandel.

contrast.why: Carignan ripens late and keeps its acidity, so both worlds grow it in heat. The Old World blends it and names the place. Chile and California bottle old vines, once used for bulk wine, alone under the grape's name.
contrast.blur: Old vine Carignan from the Languedoc, Roussillon or Priorat is now often bottled alone and can be as bright as Maule, and warm California sites give dense, savoury wines.
contrast.call: Iron and a rustic, savoury grip lean Old World; purer, juicier damson and dark cherry lean Maule or California. Both keep high acidity.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius: a little cool keeps the fruit bright.
service.glass: A Bordeaux glass, or a universal glass for a lighter, juicy style.
service.decant: Consider it for a young, firm old vine wine after tasting a sample; a light, juicy style needs none.
service.age: Most within five years; old vine wines reward five to fifteen.

with.why: acidity and grip to stand beside beans, duck and sausage
smoke, fat and paprika meet a rustic red

with.dish: Roast or braised lamb with herbs
with.why: the wine's dried thyme echoes the dish

with.dish: Charcuterie and hard sheep's milk cheese
with.why: salt and fat ease the firm tannin

labels.means: The spelling used in California, with a final e, for the same grape.
Its Spanish names: Mazuelo in Rioja, Samsó in Catalonia; Cariñena is also a place in Aragon.
Carignan of south west Sardinia, much of it from old, ungrafted bush vines in coastal sand.
A name shared by growers in Maule, Chile, for Carignan from old vines farmed without irrigation.
Old vines, in French: no age is fixed by law, but with Carignan it is the phrase to look for.

guest.q: I have never heard of Carignan. What is it like?
guest.a: A deep, tangy Mediterranean red: black raspberry and cranberry with dried thyme, bright acidity and a firm grip. If you enjoy Côtes du Rhône or Chianti, you will feel at home.

guest.q: Why do the labels make so much of old vines?
guest.a: Young Carignan crops heavily and can taste thin and harsh. Old vines give far less fruit, so the wine has the depth to carry its acidity and tannin.

guest.q: Is Cariñena a grape or a place?
guest.a: Both. It is a town and a wine region in Aragon, and it is also a Spanish name for this grape, which Rioja calls Mazuelo.

compare.tell: Grenache is paler, softer and sweeter fruited, with kirsch and low acidity; Carignan is darker, with cranberry, high acidity and firm tannin.
Mourvèdre is darker and meatier, with leather and game and only medium acidity; Carignan is tangier, with cranberry and black raspberry.

cards.front: Carignan: its names in Rioja, Catalonia, Sardinia and California?
cards.back: Mazuelo in Rioja and Samsó in Catalonia, with Cariñena elsewhere in Spain; Carignano in Sardinia; Carignane, with a final e, in California.

cards.front: What does the name VIGNO on a Chilean label promise?
cards.back: Carignan from Maule, from vines at least thirty years old, head trained and farmed without irrigation, aged two years before sale.

cards.front: Carignan blind: Old World or New World, what does a taster lean on?
cards.back: Iron, liquorice and a rustic, savoury grip lean the Languedoc, Spain or Sardinia. Purer, juicier damson and dark cherry on a finer grip lean Maule or California. Both keep high acidity.

questions.q: Two reds from old Carignan vines are poured blind, both high in acidity. The first shows black raspberry with iron, liquorice and a rustic, savoury grip; the second is juicier and purer, with damson and dark cherry on a finer grip. Which pair of origins fits, in that order?
questions.exp: Iron and a rustic, savoury grip tend to mark the Languedoc. Juicier, purer damson and dark cherry on a finer grip tend to mark old vines in Maule, so the reverse order does not fit.

questions.q: A guest sees the word Mazuelo on the back label of a Rioja and asks what it is. What do you tell her?
opts: Carignan, used in small shares for acidity and tannin
Tempranillo, under its local Rioja name
Grenache, the grape Spain calls Garnacha
Graciano, a perfumed grape native to Rioja
questions.exp: Mazuelo is the Rioja name for Carignan, a tannic, acidic grape blended in small shares. Tempranillo leads Rioja under its own name, and Garnacha and Graciano are different grapes.

questions.q: A blind red is deep ruby with a purple rim, with black raspberry, cranberry, dried thyme and liquorice. The acidity is high and the tannin is high and rustic. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: High acidity with high, rustic tannin and tangy black raspberry and cranberry point to Carignan. Grenache is paler and low in acidity, and Mourvèdre is meatier with only medium acidity.

sources.title: Decanter: Corbières, a profile of the appellation
Napa Valley Wine Academy: Chile's Carignan renaissance
The Oxford Companion to Wine, entry on Carignan

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it, though this is the thinnest side by side of the chunk. TASTE.world reads old. Trade notes on Maule describe high acidity, firm tannin, dark cherry, blackberry and dried herb, close to the Old World glass, so the contrast is written as a matter of degree, savoury and rustic against juicier and purer in fruit, and the call ends by saying that high acidity marks both. A reviewer may judge that at home and abroad would serve this grape better.
No GRID_SAY: say is kah-reen-YAHN, with kah-ree-NYEH-nah for the Spanish name; the field takes letters only, so the Spanish name itself is not written there.

The story that Chile planted Carignan in Maule after the earthquake of 1939 is left out: one page read through search states it, another calls the history an open question, and a search for a second source found none.

The share of Carignan that VIGNO asks for is left out: pages read through search give 65, 70 and 85 per cent. Vines of thirty years or more, head trained, farmed without irrigation and two years of ageing are agreed across them and are what the card states.

The Codex's records on Carignan read true and nothing here departs from them. Mazuelo, Cariñena and Samsó, Carignano del Sulcis on ungrafted bush vines in sand, and Carignane in the old mixed vineyards of California are the Codex's own reviewed facts.

Late ripening, heavy crops from young vines and the use of carbonic maceration in the south of France stand on The Oxford Companion to Wine, cited by its title, and on trade pages read through search. An origin in Aragon stands on Wine Grapes and those pages.
The ladder has two rungs and no cool one. Maule and the high hills of Corbières stand as moderate on the strength of cool nights and altitude; a checker may prefer another reading.
Violet was dropped from the New World glass: no page read through search confirmed a floral note in Maule Carignan.
No Creole dish is given: cassoulet, sausages and lamb suit the grape better than any of the seven.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after eleven fixes in one round. Mazuelo, Cariñena and Samsó, Carignano del Sulcis, the VIGNO vines of thirty years, head trained, dry farmed and two years before sale, and carbonic maceration in the Languedoc were confirmed; the call, a card and the worlds question parted the Old World from Maule by dried thyme though the Codex reads Maule Carignan of damson and dried herb, the New World cellar put every bottle on dry farmed vines and every Maule bottle under VIGNO, the twenty had old vines turn acidity into fruit, and a label made all Carignano del Sulcis old and ungrafted.
changed: lines.s20: Old vines turn that into black raspberry said that high acidity and tannin become fruit; old vines give it depth, as the guest answer on old vines says.
lines.s45: Where it began wanted the hedge the reference works keep (Aragon is the likely home); three words came out of the first sentence to keep the line at 109.
glass.ladder.0.notes: The Codex's Maule record reads its Carignan of damson and dried herb; damson takes the place of sour cherry, which the red fruit notes still hold.

worlds.contrast.old.cellar: Often fermented whole by carbonic maceration was said of the whole Old World; the Codex puts it in the Languedoc. Fermented whole keeps the intact berries the Codex's technique record describes.

worlds.contrast.new.glass: The glass gave Maule less of the dried thyme, where the Codex's Maule record reads its Carignan dark, high acid and savoury, of damson and dried herb. Juicier and purer stays; damson and a little dried thyme join it, and the finer grip is the profile's old vine silk.

worlds.contrast.new.cellar: Every bottle was said to come from dry farmed bush vines under the grape's name, and every Maule bottle to carry VIGNO, which is a guild's mark on some. Usually and some hedge it.

worlds.contrast.call: The call parted the Old World from Maule by dried thyme, which the Codex gives Maule Carignan too. Iron and a rustic grip against purer damson and dark cherry part them, and both keep high acidity.
labels.2.means: The label made every Carignano del Sulcis old and ungrafted; the rule asks for the grape and the place, and much of it comes from such vines.
cards.2.back: The card follows the call.
questions.0.q: The worlds question parted the two glasses by dried thyme as the call did; the scene now gives the first glass iron and liquorice and the second damson, dark cherry and a finer grip.
questions.0.exp: The explanation follows the stem.
open: The side by side is the thinnest of the chunk: Maule and the Languedoc differ by degree. The plan fixes contrast and names Maule in its reason; a reviewer may still judge at home and abroad the better form.
